subject: maths
title: Percentages — find, change, reverse

slides.heading: Percentages are everywhere — here is why they work
slides.body: A percentage is a fraction with denominator 100 — 'per cent' literally means 'per hundred'. Expressing things as percentages makes it easy to compare quantities with different sizes: a 30% discount on a £50 shirt and a 30% discount on a £200 coat are calculated the same way, just on different starting values.
slides.note: Maximum 3 sentences. Plain English. No AQA references. What is this and why does it matter.

slides.heading: The multiplier method — one number does it all
slides.formulaExplained: Convert the percentage to a decimal multiplier: for an increase of p%, the multiplier is 1 + p/100; for a decrease of p%, it is 1 − p/100. Applying the multiplier in one step is faster and less error-prone than finding the percentage amount separately and then adding or subtracting. To reverse a percentage change, divide by the multiplier instead of multiplying.
slides.whenToUse: For any percentage increase, decrease, or reverse percentage question — whenever a starting or ending value and a percentage are involved.
slides.note: Show formula in standard notation. Explain each variable. State when this formula applies.

slides.heading: Let's work through one
slides.question: A laptop costs £750. It is reduced by 40% in a sale. Find the sale price.

steps.instruction: Find the multiplier for a 40% reduction.
steps.working: A reduction means we keep (100% − 40%) = 60% of the original. 60 ÷ 100 = 0.60.

steps.instruction: Multiply the original price by the multiplier.
Check: find 40% of £750 separately and subtract.

slides.note: Numbers must differ from any question in the question bank for this subtopic.

slides.heading: Watch out for this

mistakes.mistake: Using 0.40 as the multiplier for a 40% reduction instead of 0.60 — multiplying by 0.40 gives the discount amount (£300), not the sale price.
mistakes.correction: A reduction multiplier = 1 − (percentage ÷ 100). For 40%: 1 − 0.40 = 0.60. Multiply by 0.60 to get the new price directly.

mistakes.mistake: Reversing a percentage change by subtracting the percentage from the new value — e.g. after a 20% rise the price is £96; student calculates £96 × 0.80 = £76.80 instead of £96 ÷ 1.20 = £80.
mistakes.correction: To reverse a percentage increase, divide the new value by the multiplier: original = new value ÷ (1 + p/100). Subtracting a percentage from the new value gives the wrong answer because the percentage is of the original, not the new value.

mistakes.mistake: Dividing by the new value instead of the original when calculating percentage change — e.g. a rise from £50 to £60: student computes (60−50)/60 × 100 = 16.7% instead of (60−50)/50 × 100 = 20%.
mistakes.correction: Percentage change = (change ÷ original) × 100. Always divide by the starting value.

slides.note: Minimum 2, maximum 3 mistakes. Specific not generic.

keyFacts.fact: To find p% of a quantity: convert p% to a decimal (p ÷ 100) and multiply by the quantity.
keyFacts.examTip: 15% of £240: 0.15 × 240 = £36. Convert first, then multiply — do not try to do it in your head as a fraction.

keyFacts.fact: Multiplier for a p% increase = 1 + p/100. Multiplier for a p% decrease = 1 − p/100.
keyFacts.examTip: A 30% increase → multiplier 1.30. A 30% decrease → multiplier 0.70. Write the multiplier before doing any calculation.

keyFacts.fact: To reverse a percentage change (find the original value): divide the new value by the multiplier. Never subtract the percentage from the new value.
keyFacts.examTip: If something costs £92.40 after a 10% discount, the original = £92.40 ÷ 0.90 = £102.67, not £92.40 − 9.24.

keyFacts.fact: Percentage change = (change ÷ original value) × 100. Always divide by the original (starting) value, not the new one.
keyFacts.examTip: The single most common mark lost in percentage change questions: dividing by the wrong value.
